rationale: The evidence pack covers Canva's developer APIs, SDKs, MCP server, and automation/integration features, but contains no mention of interactive prototyping capabilities such as animated state transitions, conditional logic, variables, or scroll-triggered effects within Canva designs. This is a fair axis for a design tool to be judged on, but nothing in the pack shows Canva delivers it.

Canva ships a documented MCP server with write-capable tools (design generation, editing, export, comments) plus Connect APIs and Apps SDK for programmatic design creation/modification, and runtime probes confirm the hosted MCP endpoint is live and speaks the MCP/OAuth flow. missing for 10: independent third-party hands-on confirmation of successful write operations (create/modify) beyond docs and a single auth-handshake probe, and no evidence of real-world community usage reports validating reliability.

Canva documents both a Connect API and an official MCP server whose tools explicitly include 'Design export: Generate exports in multiple formats (PDF, PNG, JPG, PPTX, MP4, and so on)' alongside programmatic design generation/editing, and a runtime probe confirms the hosted MCP server at mcp.canva.com is live and speaks MCP/OAuth as documented. This gives an AI agent a documented programmatic surface for rendering and exporting designs. Missing for 10: independent/hands-on confirmation of an actual successful export call (probe only reached the auth challenge) and clearer parity between MCP tools and raw Connect API export endpoints.

Canva ships an official hosted MCP server (confirmed live and OAuth-gated in the runtime probe) exposing design generation, editing, discovery, asset/brand-kit access, and export tools, which does give an agent programmatic access to some design context. However, none of the evidence mentions frames, variables, screenshots-as-spec, or component-to-code mappings — Canva's MCP is oriented toward generating/editing marketing designs, not extracting structured design specs for a coding agent to implement UI in code. Missing for 10: evidence of frame/layer-level structure, design tokens/variables, or component mapping data suitable for code implementation.

A live llms.txt is confirmed at canva.dev/llms.txt (HTTP 200), and Canva publishes extensive agent-oriented markdown docs (mcp.md, connect.md, apps.md) explicitly designed for AI tools/assistants to consume, including a documented MCP server for natural-language design tasks. Missing for 10: no independent third-party confirmation that agents successfully parse/act on llms.txt in practice.

The evidence pack shows Canva letting users import external data to drive design generation, bulk creation, and personalized template population (canva-docs-7, canva-docs-8, canva-docs-32), but nothing shows Canva's AI analyzing a user's own data to surface insights or proactive suggestions (e.g., analytics-style recommendations). This is closer to data-driven content generation than 'AI-generated insights and suggestions from my data,' so there is no concrete evidence the described capability exists.

Canva provides Connect APIs, Apps SDK, and an MCP server that let developers or AI assistants trigger design generation, personalization, and bulk creation programmatically, which could be wired into an automation pipeline, but there is no evidence of a native Canva-hosted scheduler, trigger, or background-running automation engine that executes autonomously without an external caller invoking it each time. missing for 10: evidence of a built-in trigger/scheduler or persistent background job runner, independent confirmation of autonomous (unattended) execution, and any first-party 'automation' product distinct from on-demand API/MCP calls.

Evidence mentions a 'Canva AI' feature only in passing (pasting links to add context to designs) but provides no detail on delegating broader tasks to a built-in assistant; most AI-related evidence instead describes the MCP server that lets *external* AI assistants control Canva, not an assistant embedded within Canva's own UI. missing for 10: documentation of an in-app AI assistant's task scope, examples of users delegating multi-step design tasks to it, and independent/hands-on confirmation of its capabilities.

Canva offers Connect APIs, an OpenAPI spec for client SDK generation, and a CLI that runs keylessly (verified via npm probe), enabling some automation/CI workflows; the MCP server exists but requires OAuth (401 without auth), and Canva is fundamentally a design/editor product, not built for headless batch execution as a first-class CI use case. missing for 10: evidence of a documented headless/CI mode for the Connect API itself (e.g., service-account or CI-friendly auth flow), independent confirmation of automation pipelines running unattended in CI, and clarity on whether Bulk create/design generation can run without a human editor session.

All evidence describes Canva shipping an official MCP *server* so external AI assistants can call Canva's tools (canva-docs-28, canva-probe-4, canva-probe-rt-2) — the opposite direction of this story, which asks whether Canva itself can plug in and consume external MCP servers. No evidence shows Canva acting as an MCP client that ingests third-party MCP tools.

Canva ships and documents an official hosted MCP server (mcp.canva.com) exposing design generation, editing, search, export, and comment tools to any AI assistant via natural language, and a runtime probe confirms the endpoint is live and correctly implements the MCP OAuth handshake. Missing for 10: independent/third-party hands-on confirmation of authenticated tool calls succeeding end-to-end beyond the vendor docs and initial handshake probe.

Canva ships an official hosted MCP server (mcp.canva.com) exposing design generation, editing, discovery, export, and comment tools via natural language to AI assistants, and this was confirmed live in a runtime probe (proper OAuth challenge response, not a dead endpoint). Docs explicitly describe this as giving users access to Canva's design capabilities 'through natural language, directly from the AI tools they already use.' Missing for 10: independent/hands-on end-to-end usage report showing a full natural-language command actually completing a design task (only the auth handshake was probed, not full tool invocation).

Canva ships an official CLI (`@canva/cli`) documented for creating/managing Canva apps, and a runtime probe confirms it runs keylessly via npx and reports a version, corroborating first-party docs. missing for 10: no evidence the CLI itself exposes AI-native/agentic commands (agentic access is instead delivered via the separate MCP server), and no independent third-party review of the CLI's UX.

Canva ships well-documented Connect APIs with OpenAPI description for client SDK generation, plus Apps SDK/CLI and an official hosted MCP server (confirmed live via runtime probe) enabling AI-native agents to drive design generation, editing, search, and export through natural language. This is a strong, first-party, verifiably live public API/agent surface. Missing for 10: no independent third-party corroboration of API robustness beyond vendor docs/probes, and the raw openapi.json endpoint itself 404s at guessed paths (though OpenAPI description is referenced in docs).

Canva's hosted MCP server and Connect APIs use OAuth 2.0 (protected-resource metadata, bearer tokens) rather than raw shared keys, which implies some standard OAuth consent/scoping model, and team apps let admins control who can use an app. However, the evidence pack never documents explicit least-privilege scope selection (e.g., a list of granular permission scopes an admin can assign to an agent's token) for Connect API or MCP credentials. Missing for 10: documented scope list/permission granularity for API tokens, admin UI for restricting agent credential scope, and independent confirmation that scoped tokens actually limit access in practice.
